3.  Investment Objectives

The primary objective of the portfolio is to grow multi-generational wealth with disciplined risk control and tax efficiency. The strategy is designed to support the household’s stated goals while keeping risk within the tolerance described in Section 4.

The plan is not about basic retirement funding; it is about shifting future appreciation out of the taxable estate while maintaining a high-liquidity reserve. Current assets support lifestyle spending, charitable grants, annual exclusion gifts, and private-fund capital calls with a 97% modeled success rate.

The primary objective of the portfolio is to provide reliable, inflation-aware income while preserving principal and protecting against the early-retirement risk of poor returns. 8.  Rebalancing Policy

The portfolio is monitored on an ongoing basis and rebalanced toward the policy targets in Section 6 using the following approach:

Tolerance bands: an asset class is rebalanced when it drifts outside the allowable range shown in the allocation table.

Scheduled review: allocation is reviewed at least quarterly and formally at the annual review.

Cash-flow rebalancing: contributions, withdrawals, dividends, and required distributions are directed first to bring the portfolio back toward target before trades are placed.

Tax-aware execution: in taxable accounts, rebalancing weighs the tax cost of realizing gains against the benefit of returning to target, and uses tax-loss harvesting where available.

9.  Roles & Responsibilities

Party Responsibilities Northcrest Wealth Partners Implement and monitor the strategy in this IPS; rebalance; report performance; meet with the Client; and act as a fiduciary in the Client’s best interest at all times. Client Provide accurate, timely information on goals, circumstances, and risk tolerance; fund the accounts; review reports; and notify the Advisor promptly of material changes. Charles Schwab Advisor Services Hold assets, execute trades, produce account statements and confirmations, and safeguard the Client’s property.

8.  Rebalancing Policy

The portfolio is monitored on an ongoing basis and rebalanced toward the policy targets in Section 6 using the following approach:

Tolerance bands: an asset class is rebalanced when it drifts outside the allowable range shown in the allocation table.

Scheduled review: allocation is reviewed at least quarterly and formally at the annual review.

Cash-flow rebalancing: contributions, withdrawals, dividends, and required distributions are directed first to bring the portfolio back toward target before trades are placed.

Tax-aware execution: in taxable accounts, rebalancing weighs the tax cost of realizing gains against the benefit of returning to target, and uses tax-loss harvesting where available.

9.  Roles & Responsibilities

Party Responsibilities Northcrest Wealth Partners Implement and monitor the strategy in this IPS; rebalance; report performance; meet with the Client; and act as a fiduciary in the Client’s best interest at all times. Client Provide accurate, timely information on goals, circumstances, and risk tolerance; fund the accounts; review reports; and notify the Advisor promptly of material changes. Charles Schwab Advisor Services Hold assets, execute trades, produce account statements and confirmations, and safeguard the Client’s property.

Parties and Engagement This Investment Advisory Agreement (the “Agreement”) is entered into as of May 18, 2024 (the “Effective Date”) by and between Ronald Foster and Linda Foster (individually and collectively, the “Client”) and Northcrest Wealth Partners, LLC, a registered investment adviser organized under the laws of the State of Utah (the “Adviser”). The Adviser is registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission under SEC File No. 801-118402 (CRD No. 284417). In consideration of the mutual covenants below, the parties agree as follows. By signing this Agreement the Client appoints the Adviser as a fiduciary with respect to the assets listed on Schedule A and agrees to the advisory fee described in Section 4. Reviewed progress toward “Retirement” — target $2,423,000 by 2057 (high priority).

Rebalance back to the policy targets, prioritizing cash-flow and tax-lot selection over outright sales in taxable accounts.

Hold the current allocation and risk level — no change to tolerance.

3.  Investment Objectives

The primary objective of the portfolio is to grow and progressively diversify family wealth ahead of a planned business exit, building liquidity and reducing concentration risk. The strategy is designed to support the household’s stated goals while keeping risk within the tolerance described in Section 4.

David and Susan can cover a basic retirement from existing accounts, but their preferred age-62 retirement depends on a successful sale of Nakamura Precision Tooling. The key planning issue is business concentration: more than half of family net worth is tied to one private company. Nakamura, David & Susan  ·  February 05, 2025

Date February 05, 2025 Meeting type Annual Review Attendees David Nakamura, Susan Nakamura; Marcus Devlin, CFP, CFA Prepared by Marcus Devlin, CFP, CFA (notes) Location Video conference

Discussion

Reviewed progress toward “Sell business and retire by age 62” — target $4,300,000 by 2030 (high priority).

Reviewed progress toward “Fund retirement lifestyle after business exit” — target $150,000 by 2030 (high priority).

Portfolio is roughly 53% equity against the 55% policy target; drifted modestly with the rally, agreed to trim back to target.

Refreshed the retirement projection — plan confidence (Monte Carlo) at 80%, spending target ~$150,000/yr.

Tax planning: Qualified Business Income deduction is useful but partly limited by high taxable income.

Reviewed coverage in force (Term Life, Buy-Sell Funding Life, Disability Income) for adequacy.

Business exit: Nakamura Precision Tooling, Inc. (est. $4,500,000, 80% owned) remains the central planning issue; concentration and deal-readiness discussed.

Decisions

Rebalance back to the policy targets, prioritizing cash-flow and tax-lot selection over outright sales in taxable accounts.

Hold the current allocation and risk level — no change to tolerance.

Proceed with the planned tax strategy for the year as discussed.

5.  Time Horizon

The Client is approximately age 34 with a planned retirement at age 50 (about 16 years away), followed by a multi-decade distribution phase. Funding goals span from 2028 through 2041. Because the overall horizon is long, the portfolio is managed with a multi-year orientation; near-term spending needs are met from the cash and fixed-income reserves described in Sections 6 and 7 so that growth assets are not sold into a downturn.

Patel, Priya  ·  May 18, 2025

Date May 18, 2025 Meeting type Annual Review Attendees Priya Patel; Marcus Devlin, CFP®, CFA Prepared by Marcus Devlin, CFP®, CFA (notes) Location Video conference

Discussion

Reviewed progress toward “Diversify concentrated Vertex (VCSY) position” — target $300,000 by 2028 (high priority).

Reviewed progress toward “First-home down payment” — target $250,000 by 2028 (high priority).

Portfolio is roughly 96% equity against the 85% policy target; drifted modestly with the rally, agreed to trim back to target.

Refreshed the retirement projection — plan confidence (Monte Carlo) at 90%, spending target ~$102,000/yr.

Tax planning: 10b5-1 plan adopted to sell vested VCSY on a pre-set schedule, spreading gains and removing blackout/insider timing risk.

Reviewed coverage in force (Disability (own-occupation, individual), Term Life (20-year level)) for adequacy.

Decisions

Rebalance back to the policy targets, prioritizing cash-flow and tax-lot selection over outright sales in taxable accounts.

Hold the current allocation and risk level — no change to tolerance.

Proceed with the planned tax strategy for the year as discussed.

Sutton, Mark & George  ·  June 16, 2025

Date June 16, 2025 Meeting type Annual Review Attendees Mark Sutton, George Sutton; Marcus Devlin, CFP®, CFA Prepared by Marcus Devlin, CFP®, CFA (notes) Location Video conference

Discussion

Reviewed progress toward “Retirement” — target $2,392,000 by 2059 (high priority).

Portfolio is roughly 55% equity against the 63% policy target; drifted modestly with the rally, agreed to trim back to target.

Decisions

Rebalance back to the policy targets, prioritizing cash-flow and tax-lot selection over outright sales in taxable accounts.

Hold the current allocation and risk level — no change to tolerance.

Action Items

Next review scheduled for approximately one year out. Reviewed progress toward “Retirement” — target $631,000 by 2062 (high priority).

Hold the current allocation and risk level — no change to tolerance.

5.  Time Horizon

The Client is approximately age 74 and is already in the distribution phase of retirement, with a planning horizon that extends across the remainder of both spouses’ lifetimes. Funding goals span from 2026 through 2040. Because the overall horizon is long, the portfolio is managed with a multi-year orientation; near-term spending needs are met from the cash and fixed-income reserves described in Sections 6 and 7 so that growth assets are not sold into a downturn.

Reviewed progress toward “Possible home downsize” — target $500,000 by 2027 (medium priority).

3.  Investment Objectives

The primary objective of the portfolio is to accumulate wealth toward retirement and education goals with a long-horizon growth orientation. The strategy is designed to support the household’s stated goals while keeping risk within the tolerance described in Section 4.

Peak-earning accumulators in their late 30s with two young children. Saving aggressively (~$135k/yr across 401(k), 403(b), backdoor Roths, 529s, and an invested HSA) toward retirement at 60 and fully-funded in-state college for both kids. Portfolio is intentionally growth-tilted (~80% equity) given the long horizon. Monte Carlo success 86%. Primary risks: lifestyle creep, a single-employer (RSU) concentration in Marcus's comp, and disability of Tanya (the larger earner).

4.  Risk Tolerance

Based on the household’s completed risk assessment and planning conversations, the Client’s overall risk tolerance is characterized as Growth. This tolerance reflects both the capacity to take risk (time horizon, income sources, and reserves) and the willingness to accept short-term volatility in pursuit of long-term return. The Advisor will not pursue returns that require risk beyond this level, even in strong markets.

Risk tolerance Growth Risk score (0–100) 72 Target equity exposure 80% Current equity exposure ~87%

The portfolio is monitored on an ongoing basis and rebalanced toward the policy targets in Section 6 using the following approach:

Tolerance bands: an asset class is rebalanced when it drifts outside the allowable range shown in the allocation table.

Scheduled review: allocation is reviewed at least quarterly and formally at the annual review.

Cash-flow rebalancing: contributions, withdrawals, dividends, and required distributions are directed first to bring the portfolio back toward target before trades are placed.

Tax-aware execution: in taxable accounts, rebalancing weighs the tax cost of realizing gains against the benefit of returning to target, and uses tax-loss harvesting where available.

The portfolio is monitored on an ongoing basis and rebalanced toward the policy targets in Section 6 using the following approach:

Tolerance bands: an asset class is rebalanced when it drifts outside the allowable range shown in the allocation table.

Scheduled review: allocation is reviewed at least quarterly and formally at the annual review.

Cash-flow rebalancing: contributions, withdrawals, dividends, and required distributions are directed first to bring the portfolio back toward target before trades are placed.

Tax-aware execution: in taxable accounts, rebalancing weighs the tax cost of realizing gains against the benefit of returning to target, and uses tax-loss harvesting where available.
